Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones
A specific texture associated with the event

Threat.value: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience
I study people's faces and body language to detect if they are a threat
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order

I have to be on guard all the time
The world is a dangerous place

issues.explanation: For a 55-year-old female bank teller with combat trauma, 'Bicycle' as a trigger is hard to reconcile with the rest of the profile. The other trigger items imply interpersonal/loss and sensory trauma reminders, while bicycle is a highly specific cue with no support from threat, memory, or appraisal content and no clear combat linkage. This makes it clinically implausible rather than merely unusual.

issues.item: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you
issues.explanation: 'You can never know who will harm you' is too nonspecific relative to the rest of the profile. The threat items emphasize overt vigilance and reading faces/body language, and the appraisals also center betrayal and loss of meaning. This item implies diffuse interpersonal mistrust without a corresponding interpersonal memory or trigger pattern beyond betrayal, making the negative appraisal set less coherent with the otherwise combat/loss-focused formulation.

issues.item: Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted
issues.explanation: The profile is otherwise organized around combat-linked threat, sensory triggers, and disjointed trauma memory, but the betrayal appraisal introduces a different interpersonal trauma theme that is not supported by the other selected items. With combat trauma, betrayal can occur, but here there are no corresponding triggers, memory content, or threat/appraisal items suggesting moral injury, friendly-fire, command betrayal, or interpersonal violation. This makes the betrayal item the main clinically incoherent element relative to the rest of the profile and formulation.

vignette: Maria is a 55-year-old bank teller who has been on her own since her divorce a decade ago. She lives quietly, but quiet is not the same as peaceful. The thing that shattered her was not a divorce-it was the deployment to a forward operating base in Helmand Province thirty years ago, where she served as a logistics specialist. One afternoon, an IED detonated near her convoy. The blast threw her from the vehicle; the sound was a single, percussive crack that seemed to hollow out the world. All around her were the bodies of soldiers she had shared meals with an hour before. What she remembers most vividly is the texture-the fine, gritty desert sand that caked her hands and uniform, that she could feel between her teeth for days afterward. That texture, and the faces of the dead. Now, three decades later, Maria cannot tell the story of that day without losing the thread. When a well-meaning coworker asks about her time in the service, she starts, stops, and finally gives up, the sequence jumbled so badly that even she doubts what happened. The memory itself feels unreal-a movie she once watched, not something that actually happened to her. But the uncertainty does not bring distance; it brings fear. Because she cannot trust her own memory, she has come to believe that danger could come from any direction, that she must be ready for something she cannot see coming. This is why she studies faces. Every customer who approaches her teller window is scanned for a flicker of threat-a tightened jaw, a gaze that lingers too long. She has learned to read body language the way others read headlines. The scanning never stops: she constantly surveys the bank lobby for exits, for shadows, for the wrong angle of a backpack. The world, Maria is certain, is a dangerous place. That belief was forged in the blast, but it is reinforced every day by the small things. A customer mentions losing a loved one-a parent, a spouse-and Maria feels her own loss rip open again. That moment of talk about loss does more than trigger a sad memory; it triggers a flood of physical reactivity. Her heart pounds, her palms sweat, and she suddenly has to grip the counter to stay upright. The tactile memory of desert grit returns unbidden whenever she touches certain fabrics-the rough surface of a new fleece jacket, the grain of a wooden desk drawer. And the explosion sounds: a car backfiring outside, a tray of metal utensils dropped in the break room. Every bang sends her into high alert, her body responding before her mind can catch up. The more Maria's body reacts, the more she scans. And the more she scans, the more she sees evidence that the world is hostile. She notices a customer with a tense expression and interprets it as a prelude to violence; she sees two people arguing in the parking lot and is certain that it could spill into the bank. Her hypervigilance has become a lens that tints everything dark. She has come to believe that nothing in her life matters anymore-not the friendships she let wither, not the hobbies she abandoned, not the sense of purpose she once had. What is the point, she thinks, if the world is always one snap away from breaking? This cycle has tightened over the years. The triggers keep feeding the threat monitoring; the threat monitoring keeps feeding the sense of danger; the sense of danger feeds the triggers because she now anticipates them everywhere. She finds herself avoiding certain conversations-if a coworker starts talking about a family funeral, Maria finds an excuse to walk away. She avoids the feel of any fabric that reminds her of sand. She flinches at the sound of the coin counter when it clunks loudly. Her life has shrunk to the quietest possible version: home, work, home, with the television barely audible and the curtains drawn. She finally came to a therapist after a customer slammed a cash drawer, and she dropped to the floor, trembling, in front of a line of waiting people. The shame of that moment, she says, was the worst part. But what she is most afraid of is that the memory will not stay buried-that one day it will surface so clearly that she will never be able to convince herself it was not real. Because the memory felt so strange and yet so present, she began to see its shape in ordinary things-a flash of tan fabric, a distant backfire, the way dust motes hung in the afternoon light-and each of these became a warning she could not afford to ignore. What she hopes for is a little peace, a way to walk through the world without her body screaming at every turn. And each time her body flinched, a thought arrived with the force of certainty: this is proof that danger is always here, that she will never be safe again.

violations.explanation: No paragraph directly conveys that triggers (reminders) lead to negative appraisals (distorted beliefs about danger or meaninglessness); the causal link is mediated by physical reactivity and scanning in separate paragraphs.
No paragraph directly conveys that the trauma memory leads to triggers; instead, triggers lead to memory, or memory leads to threat but not explicitly to triggers.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: No paragraph directly conveys that triggers (reminders) lead to negative appraisals (distorted beliefs about danger or meaninglessness); the causal link is mediated by physical reactivity and scanning in separate paragraphs.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Memory → Triggers: No paragraph directly conveys that the trauma memory leads to triggers; instead, triggers lead to memory, or memory leads to threat but not explicitly to triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
